title: A216_ML_2.pdf.pdf
summary: This lecture introduces the foundational concepts of Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning, clarifying their interrelationships and distinct characteristics. It defines learning as the process of improving performance on a task through experience, and outlines the typical steps in a machine learning workflow, including problem formulation, data collection, feature engineering, model selection, training, evaluation, and deployment. The session also categorizes machine learning into supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, and highlights diverse application domains from image recognition to predictive analytics. By the end of the lecture, students should be able to articulate the differences among AI, ML, and DL, describe the machine learning pipeline, and recognize the types of learning algorithms suitable for various real‑world problems.

title: A216_ML_3.pdf.pdf
summary: This lecture introduces decision trees, a hierarchical model used for classification tasks in machine learning. Students learn how to construct a tree by selecting informative attributes, evaluate its performance on a training set, and apply the resulting model to classify unseen instances. The session emphasizes the interpretability of decision trees and their suitability for practical decision-making scenarios.

summary: This lecture introduces clustering as a fundamental unsupervised learning technique, focusing on its purpose, underlying structures, and practical applications. It outlines the motivation for clustering, explains key concepts such as similarity metrics and cluster validity, and presents the K‑Means algorithm as a canonical example. Students learn to formulate clustering problems, evaluate cluster quality, and recognize when clustering can yield actionable insights.

title: ML.LEC6
summary: Lecture 6 of AI216 introduces the perceptron, the foundational binary classifier that models a single neuron, linking biological neuron structure to computational learning models. It explains how weighted inputs are summed, a bias term added, and an activation function applied to produce a discrete output, highlighting the perceptron's role as a linear decision boundary learner. Students learn the perceptron update rule, convergence guarantees for linearly separable data, and its significance as the building block for multilayer neural networks and modern pattern recognition systems.
